name: Milan Cathedral (the Duomo)
label: Duomo
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Piazza del Duomo' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Piazza del Duomo' (way/463529462): middle (413 m across); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/18017026: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Milan Cathedral' (180 m across).

text.description:
Milan Cathedral is the largest church in Italy and one of the largest in the world. It is a huge Gothic building of pale marble, crowded with spires and statues. Work started in 1386 and the final details were not finished until 1965, so it has been built, added to and tidied up over nearly six centuries. Look high on the exterior for Amadeo's Little Spire, a Renaissance addition from 1507 to 1510 that sits happily among the Gothic points around it. The cathedral stands on the site of Milan's old Roman centre, and the streets around the square still radiate from it or circle it.

It photographs well because the façade is so wide and detailed, and because the open square gives you room to step back. The classic picture is the full width of the façade filling the frame, with the main spire centred above. Early morning is the usual advice: the square is emptier and the low sun lights the marble. By day it is very busy, so expect people in the foreground. For a variation, move to another spot in the square for an angled view with the Galleria entrance in front, which shows the cathedral's depth as well as its width. Via Torino is another option, with the cathedral rising above the rooflines. Tripods and selfie sticks are not allowed in the cathedral complex, so plan on handheld shots. Right next to it: Duomo rooftop terraces.
text.geographic_location: In the very centre of Milan, on Piazza del Duomo. The Duomo Metro station is a short walk away, and the Galleria sits at the edge of the same square.
text.directions_text: Take Metro line M1 or Metro line M3 to Duomo Metro station, which is a short walk from the cathedral, to the west of it. Alternatively, ride Metro line M1 to Cordusio, a slightly longer walk. Tram 24 and tram 27 stop at Piazza Fontana, about 220 m away, and tram 12, tram 19 and tram 24 stop at Via Larga, a little further away. From any of these, head for the open square in front of the cathedral. The phone icon on the map is about 230 m west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole façade in. Use the default lens (1x) for a tighter crop of the central section. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the spires and statues.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 230 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east. From here you see the full width of the cathedral façade filling the frame, with the main spire centred above.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the central spire with the middle vertical line. Keep the phone level so the building doesn't lean backwards. For a second picture, move along the square for an angled view with the Galleria entrance in the foreground. Via Torino gives a more street-level view of the cathedral above the rooflines.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the marble to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the white stone keeps its detail. Zoom in on the spires with the telephoto and hold your elbows against your body to keep the shot steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, when the square is empty and the low sun catches the marble.

text.access_note: The square is a free public space, but the cathedral is a working place of worship, and its interior, baptistery and rooftop terraces are separate from the square, so check the official site before you go for access, tickets and dress rules.

name: Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II
label: Galleria
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/166623705: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Galleria Vittorio Emanuele Secondo' (203 m across).

text.description:
The Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II is a glass-roofed shopping arcade linking Piazza del Duomo and Piazza della Scala. It is the oldest active shopping arcade in Italy and a major Milan landmark. It was designed in 1861 and built by Giuseppe Mengoni between 1865 and 1877. Two arcades cross in an octagon, topped by a glass dome roughly 37.5 m across inside. Four barrel vaults run out from it, each crowned with a lantern. The ironwork was made by a French firm and the glass plates by Saint-Gobain.

It photographs well because everything leads the eye upward and along the length of the arcade. You get the curved glass-and-iron roof, long perspective lines and shopfronts on both sides. Under the dome, the floor has four mosaics showing the coats of arms of Turin, Florence, Rome and Milan. The Turin bull is worn into a hole by visitors who spin on it for luck. The arcade is also known as Milan's drawing room, and some of the city's oldest names are here, such as Biffi Caffè (1867) and the Borsalino hat shop (1883).

For a phone, work in layers. Take one wide shot of the dome, then a few closer shots of details such as mosaics, ironwork and shop signs. Keep the phone level, because the strong vertical and horizontal lines will show any tilt. Wait a moment for gaps in the crowd before you press the shutter.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Milan, between Piazza del Duomo and Piazza della Scala. It sits right beside the Duomo and across from Teatro alla Scala.
text.directions_text: From Duomo Metro station (Metro line M1 and Metro line M3), the Galleria is to the north-east, about 3 minutes on foot. From Cordusio Metro station (Metro line M1) it is to the east, about 5 minutes on foot. By tram 1, get off at Teatro alla Scala, where the Galleria is to the south and about 3 minutes on foot away. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the dome and the curve of the glass roof. Use the default lens (1x) for the long view down the arcade. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for mosaics, statues and shop details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Stand here and let the arcade open out around you, then turn slowly to compare the views in each direction.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and line them up with the shopfront edges so the verticals stay straight. Hold the phone level and tilt it up gently for the dome. Tilting too far makes the walls lean inwards. For a symmetrical shot, centre the arcade between the two rows of shops and let the roof lines converge. For a floor detail, use the telephoto on one of the mosaics.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a bright part of the roof or on a shopfront and slide the exposure slider down a little if the glass looks washed out. Turn on night mode for evening shots, but hold the phone against a wall or rail or brace your elbows to keep it steady. A Live Photo can help if people walk through your frame, because you can pick a cleaner moment afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the morning usually means fewer people. Daylight comes through the glass roof, so it is bright in the middle of the day. In the evening the shop windows glow, which gives warmer, moodier shots.

text.access_note: It is a shopping arcade open as a public walkway between two piazzas, but check the official site before you go for any opening or access restrictions.

name: Sforza Castle
label: Sforza Castle
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Piazza Castello' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Piazza Castello' (way/728204530): edge nearest the subject (653 m across); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/1918: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Sforza Castle' (395 m across).

text.description: Sforza Castle is the big brick fortress at the edge of Milan's historic centre. Francesco Sforza built it in the 15th century on the remains of an earlier 14th-century fortification. Today it houses several of the city's museums. It photographs well because the front is wide, symmetrical and easy to read. The tall central Filarete Tower sits over the main gate, flanked by round corner towers and long red walls. The tower was rebuilt between 1900 and 1905 from 16th-century drawings, after the original was lost. In front, the semi-circular Piazza Castello was laid out in the Napoleonic period, and it leaves enough open space to step back and fit the whole front into the frame. The fountain in the middle of the square gives you a foreground, which stops the picture looking flat. Behind the castle, Parco Sempione now covers the old parade ground, and it offers a second, calmer view. From the pond you can catch the castle rising behind the water, with trees reflected in it. If you only have time for one picture, make it the classic postcard view of the tower and gate with the fountain in front. Take a few steps left or right until the tower sits centrally above the gate and the fountain.
text.geographic_location: Sforza Castle sits at the edge of Milan's historic centre, between Piazza Castello and Parco Sempione. It lies at the end of Via Dante, on the way from the Duomo, and is a short walk from Cairoli.
text.directions_text: From Cairoli (Metro line M1), the castle is to the north-west and about 4 minutes on foot. From Lanza (Metro line M2) it is about 4 minutes on foot to the south-west. You can also take tram 4 to the Piazza Castello (Cairoli M1) stop, about 3 minutes from the castle. The phone icon on the map is about 120 m south-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole front and the fountain in one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look at the tower and gate. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the top of the Filarete Tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 120 m south-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-west. The castle lies to the north-west of you. From here you see the Filarete Tower and the main gate, with the fountain in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the Filarete Tower up with a vertical line so it does not lean. Keep the fountain low in the frame as a foreground and leave the tower and gate in the middle. If you want a quieter alternative, walk into Parco Sempione and photograph the castle behind the pond, with the trees reflected in the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the brickwork to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky does not wash out. Keep your phone level, as tilting it makes the tower look as if it is falling backwards. Use the ultra-wide only if you need it, because it can stretch things at the edges of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Golden hour, according to one photo guide, when the light on the brick is warm.

text.access_note: Piazza Castello is a free public square, but the castle's museums and any other parts inside may be ticketed or restricted, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Ultra-wide lenses on phones can stretch objects near the edges of the frame.
Phone gridlines help keep tall buildings from leaning in the photo.
Lowering the exposure slider can stop a bright sky washing out when photographing the brickwork.

name: Teatro alla Scala
label: La Scala
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Piazza della Scala' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Piazza della Scala' (relation/6552703): middle (124 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/6552704: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Teatro alla Scala' (156 m across).
notes: 'la scala' alone also means other places and brands.

text.description:
Teatro alla Scala is Milan's famous opera house, and its pale, restrained neoclassical front is easy to recognise. It opened on 3 August 1778 on the site of a church, Santa Maria della Scala, which gave the theatre its name. It was badly damaged by bombing in 1943 and reopened on 11 May 1946. Today it seats 1,987 people, and its season traditionally opens on 7 December, the feast day of Milan's patron saint.

The building itself is quite sober, so the best photo comes from adding some context. Stand in Piazza della Scala near the Leonardo da Vinci monument and face the theatre's north-west facade. The statue sits in the foreground and the theatre fills the background, with Palazzo Marino across the square. That gives you a picture with a clear subject and a sense of place. The square is pedestrian, so you can step back and take your time, though expect other visitors to be doing the same.

Take one frame with the statue and facade together, then a second, tighter one of the facade alone. If you are in the area after dark, a late-night view from across the square, when the building is quiet, makes a calm, atmospheric picture. Only the outside is covered here: inside, photography is restricted and you need to check before going.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Milan, on Piazza della Scala, with Palazzo Marino on the opposite side of the square. It is a short walk from the Duomo area.
text.directions_text: The nearest tram 1 stop is Teatro alla Scala, about 1 minute on foot from the theatre. From Cordusio Metro station (Metro line M1), walk north-east for about 5 minutes on foot. From Duomo Metro station (Metro line M1 and Metro line M3), walk north for about 6 minutes on foot. Then head for the Leonardo da Vinci monument in the middle of the square. The phone icon on the map is about 35 m south-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the statue-and-facade view. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you cannot fit the whole front in, and use telephoto (2x or more) for details of the facade.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 35 m south-east of the subject, in Piazza della Scala (the phone icon on the map), and face north-west. Face north-west towards the theatre's facade, with the statue in the foreground and Palazzo Marino across the square.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the statue on one side and the theatre in the rest of the frame. Keep your phone level so the vertical lines of the facade stay straight. If you want a plainer, more formal shot, move a few steps back and frame just the facade.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the building's detail is kept. At night, use night mode and hold the phone against something steady or brace your elbows.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daytime gives you the clearest view of the facade. For a quieter, more atmospheric picture, try a late-night view from across the square, when the building is quiet.

text.access_note: The square outside is a pedestrian public space; the theatre interior, museum and performances are ticketed and photography inside is restricted, so check the official site before you go.

The ultra-wide lens (0.5x) helps fit the whole facade in when you are close, but can stretch the edges of the frame.
The square is likely to have other visitors taking photographs during the day.

name: Navigli canals
label: Navigli
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Vicolo dei Lavandai' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Vicolo Lavandai' (roads).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/3340142: large area 'Naviglio Grande' (42529 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.

text.description:
The Naviglio Grande was the most important of Milan's navigli and ends at the Darsena (Porta Ticinese dock). The canal was dug by hand over many decades. It reached Milan in 1258 and was fully navigable from 1272. Boats then carried goods in and out of the city, including stone and marble for the Duomo, whose construction began in 1386. The last cargo of sand was unloaded at the Darsena on 30 March 1979, and today the canal is used for irrigation. It is about 12 m wide as it enters the dock.

For a phone photographer, the appeal is the long, straight water lined with tall canal-side houses, plus the reflections. A good place to start is Vicolo dei Lavandai, a small alley just off the canal. It has the old communal washhouse, with its stone washbasins and historic plaques, set against the water and the row of houses behind. It is a small, lesser-known historic corner that works well as part of a canal walk.

If you have time, two other spots along the canal are worth a look. Ponte di Pietra gives a view along the canal with its pastel houses. Pont de Ferr is an iron bridge with a more industrial look. Evenings can be busy, and on the last Sunday of each month an antiques market can crowd or block the views.
text.geographic_location: The Navigli canals lie in the south-west of central Milan, around the Darsena dock and the Porta Ticinese and Porta Genova area. The Naviglio Grande runs west from the Darsena, and Vicolo dei Lavandai is a small lane just off it.
text.directions_text: The easiest start is Porta Genova Metro station on Metro line M2, about 5 minutes on foot from the phone icon on the map. Tram 2 also serves the area. The stop Via Valenza - Alzaia Naviglio Grande is about 3 minutes on foot away, and Ripa di Porta Ticinese - Via Lombardini is about 4 minutes. From the phone icon on the map, the main stretch of the Naviglio Grande lies to the west. The phone icon on the map is about 640 m east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the washhouse and the canal. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the alley feels tight. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for reflections and details such as the washbasins and plaques.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 640 m east of the subject, on Vicolo dei Lavandai (the phone icon on the map), and face west. The place to shoot from is Vicolo dei Lavandai, just off the Naviglio Grande. From the alley you can photograph the old communal washhouse with its stone washbasins and historic plaques. The canal and the lined houses behind it make a natural backdrop.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and use the washbasins as a foreground, with the canal and the houses behind. Keep the verticals straight so the houses don't lean. For a second view, walk to Ponte di Pietra and shoot along the canal, with the houses and their reflections in the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the facades to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the sky and the lit walls keep their colour. In the evening, let night mode work, and hold the phone steady against a wall or railing.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Golden hour, when the low sun lights the facades and the water along the alley. Evenings are popular, especially around Ponte di Pietra, so arrive early if you want clear views.

text.access_note: The alley and the canal-side paths are public spaces with no ticket mentioned, but the monthly antiques market on the last Sunday can block views, so check the official site before you go.

name: Bosco Verticale
label: Bosco Verticale
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Piazza Gae Aulenti' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Piazza Gae Aulenti' (way/724414223): middle (335 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/11155707089: the OpenStreetMap point 'Vertical Forest'.

text.description:
The Bosco Verticale (Vertical Forest) is a pair of residential towers in Milan's Porta Nuova district, designed by Boeri Studio and inaugurated in 2014. The towers stand 116 metres and 84 metres tall. Their façades carry hundreds of trees, thousands of shrubs and over ninety plant species, so the buildings look more like wooded hillsides than glass blocks. That mix of straight architecture and soft greenery is why they photograph so well, and the colour changes with the seasons.

The classic view is from the raised square, Piazza Gae Aulenti, where both towers sit above the fountain pools, with the UniCredit Tower at the right edge of the frame. The water adds reflections, and the raised ground gives you a clean foreground and a clear line of sight. If you have time, Biblioteca degli Alberi shows the towers among young trees. Via Gaetano de Castillia lets you look up the façades from the base.

Both towers are private homes, so you can only photograph them from outside, from public ground. Keep your phone level so the tall edges stay straight, and take a few frames at different zoom settings, as the planting looks very different close up and far away.
text.geographic_location: The towers are in the Porta Nuova district, on the edge of the Isola neighbourhood, between Via Federico Confalonieri and Via Gaetano de Castillia. They sit just north of Piazza Gae Aulenti and the Garibaldi station area.
text.directions_text: The easiest start is Isola, on Metro line M5. The towers are to the south, about 230 m away. You can also arrive at Garibaldi FS (Metro line M2 and Metro line M5) and walk north-east, about 340 m. The phone icon on the map is on Piazza Gae Aulenti, a little south of the towers, so go up to the raised square for the classic view. The phone icon on the map is about 240 m south of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in both towers and the fountain pools. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details of the planted balconies. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a lot of foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 240 m south of the subject, in Piazza Gae Aulenti (the phone icon on the map), and face north. On the upper ring at the east-side ramp of the raised square.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the tall edges of the towers up with the vertical lines, keeping the phone upright to limit leaning. Put the fountain water in the lower part of the frame for reflections. For a different version, try Biblioteca degli Alberi, where the towers appear among young trees with a green foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the towers to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky stays blue and the foliage keeps its colour. Take a few frames in case people walk through.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, before about 8 am, gives softer light and fewer people, according to one photo guide. Sunrise times change through the year, so check before you go.

text.access_note: Piazza Gae Aulenti is an open public square, but the towers are private homes, so shoot from public ground only. Drone use in Milan is restricted, so check the official rules before you go.

name: Arco della Pace
label: Arco della Pace
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Piazza Sempione' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Piazza Sempione' (way/728721234): middle (285 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/18237405: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Casello del Dazio' (49 m across).

text.description:
The Arco della Pace is a large white neoclassical arch that closes the long view down Corso Sempione, with Simplon Park and the Sforza Castle behind it. It photographs well because it is so symmetrical. The tree-lined avenue and the tram tracks run straight towards it, so a centred shot nearly composes itself. Close up, you can pick out the statues, columns and carved reliefs on the arch.

The architect Luigi Cagnola began the arch in 1807, under Napoleonic rule, to mark where the new road over the Simplon Pass entered Milan. Work stopped when the Austrians took over. Cagnola restarted it in 1826 for Emperor Francis II, who dedicated it to the 1815 Congress of Vienna. After Cagnola died in 1833, Francesco Londonio and Francesco Peverelli finished it in 1838. It stands about 25 m high and 24 m wide, so it is big enough to fill a phone frame even from some way back.

Trams and traffic pass all the time, so you may need to wait a moment for a clear shot. Take the first photo straight on from the avenue, then try a second from a different spot, such as the far end of the park, for a view with trees and lawn in front. Look at the gridlines on your screen to keep the arch's columns upright and the tracks centred.
text.geographic_location: The arch stands in Piazza Sempione, in the Porta Sempione district, part of Milan's historic centre (Zone 1). It sits at the end of Corso Sempione, with Simplon Park and the Sforza Castle on the other side of it.
text.directions_text: The easiest way is tram 1 or tram 10 to the Arco della Pace stop, about 3 minutes on foot, with the arch to the south-east of the stop. From Lanza Metro station on Metro line M2 it is about 850 m on foot, heading north-west. From Moscova Metro station, also on Metro line M2, it is about 890 m on foot, heading west. The phone icon on the map is about 35 m south-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a straight-on, symmetrical shot of the arch. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the whole avenue, the tram tracks and plenty of sky. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the longer views from across the park, where the arch looks closer and tighter.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 35 m south-west of the subject, in Piazza Sempione (the phone icon on the map), and face north-east. On the Corso Sempione axis in front of the arch. From here you see the arch straight on, framed by the tree-lined avenue, with the tram tracks leading to it. Keep to the pavement or the central promenade and do not stand in the road, as trams and traffic pass constantly.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Centre the arch and line up the tram tracks so they run into the middle of the frame. Switch on the gridlines to keep the columns upright. For a different view, try Piazza del Cannone at the far end of the park, zoomed in with trees and lawn in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the arch to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the pale stone or the sky looks washed out. If a tram is about to arrive, a Live Photo lets you pick the best moment afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Check on the day. The decorated front of the arch may face the sun in the morning, while other guides prefer late afternoon or golden hour. If you can, try both and compare.

text.access_note: The arch stands in an open public square surrounded by trams and traffic; check the official site before you go if you want anything beyond viewing it from outside.

name: Santa Maria delle Grazie
label: S. Maria delle Grazie
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Via Caradosso' (1 web pages); placed at the stretch of Via Caradosso nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/19382652: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Chiesa di Santa Maria delle Grazie' (93 m across).
notes: The church outside; the Last Supper inside is not the subject (photo rules not checked).

text.description: Santa Maria delle Grazie is a Dominican church and convent in Milan, and a UNESCO World Heritage Site. It is best known for Leonardo da Vinci's mural of The Last Supper, which is inside the refectory. For a phone photographer the building itself is the subject. Warm brick walls, a Renaissance dome and the quieter side of the church give you plenty to work with from outside. The Gothic nave was finished by 1469 under the Sforza dukes. Ludovico Sforza later had the apse and cloister rebuilt, work completed after 1490, and the design of the apse is attributed to Donato Bramante, though some dispute this. The church was hit by an aerial bombardment on the night of 15 August 1943, and much of the refectory was destroyed. The wall holding The Last Supper survived, and it had been sand-bagged for protection. Via Caradosso is a suggested street for a side angle, a different view from the usual head-on shots from the square, but check the exact corner on the map. If you want the classic view, the open Piazza di Santa Maria delle Grazie shows the brick facade and dome rising above the square. The quiet Chiostro delle Rane cloister, with its arcades and fountain topped by bronze frogs, is another option. Photography is banned in the refectory, and tripods are not allowed inside the church, so plan on exterior and cloister pictures.
text.geographic_location: Santa Maria delle Grazie stands in Milan, about 465 m from Sant'Ambrogio Metro station. Via Caradosso is a suggested street for a side angle, but its exact corner should be checked on the map.

From Sant'Ambrogio (Metro line M2 and Metro line M4) it is to the north, about 465 m on foot. text.description:
Villa Necchi Campiglio is a 1930s town house in the middle of Milan, now run as a house museum. Piero Portaluppi, a leading Milanese Rationalist architect, designed it, and it was built between 1932 and 1935 for Angelo Campiglio and the Necchi sisters. Its clean lines, glass veranda and calm garden make a refreshing change from the busy streets around it. The garden also has a tennis court and a swimming pool. The pool was the first to be built on private land in Milan, and the second in the city after the municipal one. The family left the villa to FAI, the Italian heritage trust, which restored it and opened it to visitors in May 2008. Film fans may recognise it from I Am Love and House of Gucci.

The best photograph is taken poolside in the garden, looking towards the pergola and the glazed veranda. The water, the planting and the house together give you a different angle from the usual front view. It is also a quieter corner of the grounds. Keep the lines of the veranda straight against the gridlines and let the pool fill the lower part of the frame. For a second picture, step back for the front of the house, with its entrance portico and glass veranda framed by greenery. The garden is inside the grounds, so check the official site before you go for entry and photography rules.
text.geographic_location: The villa is at via Mozart 14, in a central, serene, tree-lined residential area of Milan, between Palestro and San Babila Metro stations. It sits behind its own garden.
text.directions_text: From Palestro Metro station (Metro line M1), the villa is to the south, about 370 m on foot. From San Babila Metro station (Metro line M1 or Metro line M4), it is to the north-east, about 390 m on foot. You can also get off tram 9 or tram 19 at Piazza Tricolore, with the villa to the west, about 410 m on foot. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the veranda up with the horizontal lines. Put the water in the lower third and the house in the upper part. For a second view, use the front of the house, where the entrance portico and glass veranda sit among the greenery.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the veranda to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the bright sky and the glass keep their detail. If you see reflections in the glass, move a step to one side and try again.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft daylight, such as morning or late afternoon or a bright overcast day, usually suits the pale walls and the water better than harsh midday sun.

text.access_note: The garden is part of a ticketed FAI house museum, so check the official site before you go for opening days, entry and photography rules.
claims_not_in_sources: Soft morning, late-afternoon or bright overcast light generally suits pale walls and water better than harsh midday sun.

name: Parco Sempione
label: Parco Sempione
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Piazza del Cannone' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Piazza del Cannone' (way/120248977): middle (336 m across).

text.description: Parco Sempione is Milan's big city-centre park, tucked behind the Sforza Castle. It was laid out between 1888 and 1894 on the old parade ground, with avenues, a lake and lawns in the style of an English landscape park. It covers roughly 386,000 square metres and is fenced all round. For a phone photo, its strength is the long view across open grass and trees to the Arco della Pace at the far end. This gives you a simple, layered picture: green lawn and trunks in front, the pale arch in the distance. The park also holds the Palazzo dell'Arte, the Arena Civica and the Torre Branca, so there is plenty to fill a wider frame. The Ponte delle Sirenette, a small bridge with bronze mermaids, makes a charming close-up. It once stood over one of Milan's canals and was saved when the canal was covered over in 1930. Start at Piazza del Cannone, between the castle and the park, and look along the park towards the arch. Keep the horizon level and let the lawn take up the lower part of the picture. If people wander through, wait a moment for a gap. For a frame with only park in it, move a little further in among the trees, because the square itself is not park ground. Come back to the bridge and pond for a second, quieter picture.
text.geographic_location: Parco Sempione lies in central Milan, just north-west of the Sforza Castle. It stretches towards the Arco della Pace and the start of Corso Sempione.
text.directions_text: Cadorna FN (Metro line M1 and Metro line M2) is about 600 m on foot from the park, which lies to the north. Lanza (Metro line M2) is about 575 m away, with the park to the west. Alternatively, take tram 1 or tram 10 to the Via Pagano Via Canova stop, about 420 m on foot, with the park to the east of the stop. The phone icon on the map is about 290 m south-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the view along the park to the arch. Switch to 2x or more, if your phone has a telephoto lens, to bring the arch closer without walking. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the lawns and trees, or for the bridge and pond.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 290 m south-east of the subject, in Piazza del Cannone (the phone icon on the map), and face north-west. From here the Arco della Pace is framed at the far end of a long stretch of lawn and trees, with the park in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and place the arch on the centre line, with a few trees at the sides to make a frame. Keep your phone upright so the sides of the arch do not lean. Try one wide shot at 1x, then one tighter at 2x or more. For a different view, walk to Piazza Sempione to see the arch rising above the tree line, or go to the Ponte delle Sirenette and photograph the bridge from low down by the water so the pond fills the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the arch to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky does not wash out the stonework. If the sky looks flat, take one more frame with the exposure slightly brighter and choose the better one.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the day is usually calmer, with fewer people crossing your view. Weekends, especially near the arch, can bring performers and crowds that affect your framing.

text.access_note: The park is a fenced public park, but check the official site before you go for current opening times and whether the pond and bridge area is open.

name: Via Monte Napoleone
label: Monte Napoleone
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Via Monte Napoleone' (2 web pages); placed at crossing of Via Monte Napoleone and Via Borgospesso (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/4868904: the middle of the OpenStreetMap line 'Via Monte Napoleone' (115 m long).

text.description:
Via Monte Napoleone is an upscale shopping street in Milan, at the heart of the Quadrilatero della moda, the fashion district. It is lined with Neoclassical palaces, mostly rebuilt in the early 19th century, and today the street is known for luxury fashion houses, boutiques and jewellery retailers. The street takes its name from a public-debt bank that opened here in 1783 and was renamed the Monte Napoleone in 1804, when Milan was capital of the Napoleonic Italian Republic. Caffè Cova, founded in 1817, moved here in 1950, and Palazzo del Monte was bought by Kering in 2024.

It photographs well because the street is fairly straight and narrow, with tall facades on both sides. A phone shot taken straight down its length shows rows of shopfronts leading the eye away from you, with a few pedestrians to give a sense of scale. The phone icon on the map is at the Via Borgospesso junction, looking south-east along the street. Keep your phone level so the building edges stay upright. Two other corners are worth a look if you have time: Via Manzoni, where the boutique frontages and the junction fit in one frame, and Via Pietro Verri, good for shop windows and seasonal decorations. After dusk the lit windows add colour, though the street is busiest in fashion week and over the holidays.
text.geographic_location: In central Milan, in the Quadrilatero della moda, running between Via Alessandro Manzoni and Piazza San Babila.
text.directions_text: Take Metro line M1 or Metro line M4 to San Babila Metro station, then walk north-west into the street; the street is about 215 m from the station. Alternatively, take Metro line M3 to Montenapoleone Metro station, or tram 1 to the Montenapoleone M3 stop, and walk south-east to reach the street, about 5 minutes on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 220 m north-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the full view down the street. Try telephoto (2x or 3x, depending on your phone) to bring the shopfronts closer together, and the ultra-wide (0.5x) for a single grand facade.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 220 m north-west of the subject, at the corner of Via Monte Napoleone and Via Borgospesso (the phone icon on the map), and face south-east. You will see the whole length of the street running away from you, lined with boutique facades.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Shoot straight down the middle of the street and switch on the gridlines, so the verticals of the buildings stay straight and the street sits centrally. Wait for a gap in the pedestrians, or keep a few in for scale. For a different view, try the corner at Via Manzoni or the Via Pietro Verri junction.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the far end of the street to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so bright windows and the sky do not wash out. After dusk, use night mode and hold the phone steady against a lamp post or your body.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: After dusk, when the shop windows are lit. Expect more people during fashion week and the holiday season.

text.access_note: The street is an open public street, but the shops are private businesses, so check the official site of any shop or café before you go inside.

name: Colonne di San Lorenzo
label: Colonne di San Lorenzo
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Basilica di San Lorenzo Maggiore' (1 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/740215877: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Colonne di San Lorenzo' (58 m across).

text.description:
Sixteen tall Roman columns stand in a row in front of the Basilica di San Lorenzo Maggiore in central Milan. The columns are Corinthian and were moved to this spot in the 4th century. They were probably taken from a 2nd-century pagan temple or public bathhouse. They have survived a lot since then. In the 16th century there was a proposal to take them down so a royal procession could pass more easily, but it was turned down. Until 1935 old houses crowded right up against the church front, so the open view you see today is fairly recent.

For photos, the appeal is the contrast between weathered stone columns and the church behind them, with city life all around. Street-level shots often pick up shops, apartments and traffic behind the columns, and a bronze statue of Constantine in the middle of the piazza can drift into the frame. The square also fills with people in the evening and in summer, so early morning is the calmest time.

The phone icon on the map is at the columns themselves, so you can shoot the stonework up close. For a different angle, the basilica's forecourt lets you look back towards the columns from the church side, a little away from the street. If you want the full row of columns with the church facade behind, the Piazza di San Lorenzo is the alternative. Take a few frames from each.
text.geographic_location: The columns are in central Milan, directly in front of the Basilica di San Lorenzo Maggiore, near Corso di Porta Ticinese.
text.directions_text: The nearest Metro station is Vetra Metro station on Metro line M4, about 3 minutes on foot; the columns are to the north-west of it. De Amicis Metro station on Metro line M4 is about 5 minutes on foot, with the columns to the east. If you prefer a tram, tram 3 stops at Colonne di San Lorenzo (about 2 minutes on foot, columns to the north) and at Carrobio (about 2 minutes on foot, columns to the south). The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from where you stand for a natural view of the columns with the basilica around them. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the whole row in one frame, or use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the column tops and the arch of stone detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. For a second viewpoint, walk to the basilica's forecourt (the sagrato) and turn round to look back towards the columns. From there you get them seen from the church side, a quieter view than the one from the street or the square.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the columns with the vertical lines so they stand straight. Let the nearest column act as a frame on one side and the rest of the row lead the eye along. Try to keep shop signs and parked vehicles out of the background by shifting a step or two sideways. For the full row with the church facade behind, walk out to Piazza di San Lorenzo and take a second shot there with ultra-wide.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the columns keep their colour and texture. Hold the phone level when using ultra-wide so the columns do not lean inwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, when the square is quietest and there is less traffic and fewer people in the frame.

text.access_note: The columns stand in an open public square; the basilica's opening hours can vary, so check the official site before you go if you plan to go inside.
claims_not_in_sources: Tilting a phone upwards, especially on the ultra-wide lens, makes vertical lines such as columns appear to lean inwards.
Dragging the exposure slider down on a phone helps keep detail when the sky is bright.

name: Basilica of Sant'Ambrogio
label: Sant'Ambrogio
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Piazza Sant'Ambrogio' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Piazza Sant'Ambrogio' (way/396868526): point nearest the subject (195 m long).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/37717: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Basilica of Sant'Ambrogio' (157 m across).

text.description:
Sant'Ambrogio is one of the oldest churches in Milan. St Ambrose commissioned it between 379 and 386, and the building you see today took its look in the 12th century, when it was rebuilt in the Romanesque style. That makes it a good change from Milan's grander, later landmarks. The brickwork is warm and uneven, the arches are rounded, and the carved capitals under the porch are full of lions, boars and small human faces.

The facade is what makes the photo. A low porch sits in front, with two tiers of arches above it, and the bishops once blessed the crowds from the upper loggia. Two bell towers of different heights stand either side. The right-hand one, the Torre dei Monaci, dates from the 9th century and looks sturdy and plain. The taller left-hand one dates from 1144, with its top two floors added in 1889. The mismatch gives the picture character.

The best outdoor view is in Piazza Sant'Ambrogio, in front of the facade, looking towards the church. From there the whole front fits in one frame, with the towers and porch set in a fairly quiet square. If you want a more symmetrical shot, the arched colonnade of the Atrio di Ansperto frames the facade and both towers. Inside, the nave leads towards the golden altar and its canopy, but flash is not allowed, so keep it switched off.
text.geographic_location: The basilica is in central Milan. It stands on its own square, with the Sant'Ambrogio Metro station close by.
text.directions_text: Take Metro line M2 or Metro line M4 to Sant'Ambrogio Metro station. The basilica is a short walk of about 219 metres to the east. If you arrive at De Amicis on Metro line M4, the church is to the north and the walk is a little longer. Tram 16 and tram 19 stop at Largo D'Ancona and Corso Magenta - Via Nirone, both to the south and south-west of the church. The phone icon on the map is about 50 m west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole facade. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close or want to include the porch and the sky. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the tops of the towers and the loggia arches.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 50 m west of the subject, in Piazza Sant'Ambrogio (the phone icon on the map), and face east. In front of the facade, shooting towards the church. From here the full facade, both bell towers and the porch fit in one frame, with the quiet square around them.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the central doorway up with the middle of the frame, so the two towers balance on either side. Keep your phone level so the vertical lines stay straight; if you tilt it upwards, the towers will lean inwards. For a more symmetrical alternative, step into the arched colonnade of the Atrio di Ansperto and shoot the facade through the arches. Inside, hold the phone steady and aim down the nave towards the altar, without flash.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brick facade to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the brickwork stays rich and the sky is not blown out. Take a couple of frames, as people often walk across the square.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon usually gives the facade a warm, even light. Crowds in the square vary, so a quiet moment is worth waiting for. Interior photos are only possible during visiting times.

text.access_note: This is a working place of worship, so check the official site for visiting times and entry rules before you go, and check on arrival for access to the square.
claims_not_in_sources: The facade faces roughly west, so it is likely to catch the afternoon and evening light.
Brickwork usually looks richer if the exposure is lowered slightly against a bright sky.

name: Cimitero Monumentale
label: Cimitero Monumentale
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Piazzale Cimitero Monumentale' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Piazzale Cimitero Monumentale' (way/266873739): middle (107 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/4915384: large area 'Cimitero Monumentale' (905 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.

text.description:
The Cimitero Monumentale is one of Milan's two largest cemeteries and is known for its many artistic tombs and monuments. Carlo Maciachini designed it to bring together several small cemeteries that were scattered around the city, and it officially opened in 1866. Inside you will find sculpture, Greek-style temples, tall obelisks and even a scaled-down version of Trajan's Column. It also has the crematorium temple, which opened in 1876 and was the first crematorium in the Western world.

For a phone photo, start outside on the square. The main entrance is the Famedio, a large marble hall in a Neo-Medieval style, and its striped black, white and pink facade is the best-known view. It is also the burial place of the writer Alessandro Manzoni. From the square you can take in the whole facade, framed by the entrance, which you can't do once you are up close. If you go in, the tall white spiral tower, listed as the Bernocchi mausoleum, is a good second shot, seen from below against the sky.

This is a working cemetery, so please be quiet and respectful. Funerals and mourners come first, so lower your phone if a ceremony is under way. Flash and drones are not allowed, and tripods need permission from the cemetery office, so plan to shoot handheld.
text.geographic_location: The Cimitero Monumentale is in northern central Milan, around Piazzale Cimitero Monumentale and Via Bramante. The Monumentale stop on Metro line M5 is right beside it.
text.directions_text: Take Metro line M5 to Monumentale Metro station; the cemetery is about 2 minutes on foot to the north-west. Tram 10 also stops at Monumentale M5, about 3 minutes on foot away, and at Piazzale Cimitero Monumentale Via Bramante, about 3 minutes on foot. Cenisio Metro station on Metro line M5 is another option, about 9 minutes on foot, with the cemetery to the east. The phone icon on the map is about 200 m east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from the square to get the whole Famedio facade and its entrance. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you are very close or want a lot of sky. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the marble stripes and carved details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 200 m east of the subject, in Piazzale Cimitero Monumentale (the phone icon on the map), and face west. Outside the main gate and facing the Famedio. From here the striped black, white and pink marble facade is framed by the entrance, and it looks best from a distance on the square rather than up close.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the Famedio up in the centre of the frame, keeping the verticals straight so the facade doesn't lean. Leave a little space around the entrance so the gateway frames it. For a closer alternative, go inside and shoot straight on at the Famedio and its central dome with the entrance stairs below. The tall white spiral tower, listed as the Bernocchi mausoleum, is another option: hold your phone low and shoot upwards against the sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the pale marble keeps its detail and the pink and black stripes stay rich. Do not use flash. Keep the phone quiet and discreet, and put it away during any ceremony.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late morning, between 10 a.m. and noon, gives good directional light on the Famedio facade.

text.access_note: The square outside is public, but the Famedio and the grounds are inside the cemetery, and opening times may vary, so check the official site before you go.

name: San Bernardino alle Ossa
label: San Bernardino
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/39349468: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Chiesa di San Bernardino alle Ossa' (58 m across).

text.description:
San Bernardino alle Ossa is a Baroque church in central Milan, best known for its ossuary: a small chapel whose walls are almost entirely covered with arranged skulls and bones. The story goes back to 1210, when a room was built to hold bones from an overcrowded cemetery. A church followed in 1269, and after a fire in 1712 a larger church was built and dedicated to Saint Bernardino of Siena. The present façade was finished in 1776. Inside, the plan is octagonal, and the ossuary vault carries a fresco by Sebastiano Ricci from 1695, which is a good counterpoint to the bone-lined walls.

It photographs well because of that contrast: bones set in neat patterns in niches, around doors and along cornices, with a painted ceiling of angels above. The space is small, so think in details rather than one big view. Try a wide shot to show the whole chamber, then move in on a niche, a doorway or the vault. Outside, the church sits in a built-up part of the centre, so the façade is best caught as a simple, straight-on picture. Keep your phone upright and use the gridlines so the vertical lines stay straight. As this is a place of worship and a place of remembrance, be quiet and unhurried, and keep other visitors out of your shots where you can.
text.geographic_location: San Bernardino alle Ossa is in the centre of Milan, close to Piazza Fontana and Via Larga.
text.directions_text: From Sforza-Policlinico Metro station (Metro line M4), the church is about 431 m to the north. From San Babila Metro station (Metro line M1 or Metro line M4) it is about 446 m to the south. The nearest tram stops are Piazza Fontana (tram 24 and tram 27) and Via Larga (tram 12, tram 19 and tram 24), each about 2 minutes on foot. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the cramped interior and for the façade from close range. Use the default lens (1x) for most shots. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the bone patterns and the ceiling fresco.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. For the exterior, stand back on the pavement to fit the façade in. For the ossuary, stand just inside the doorway of the chapel for the widest view of the walls.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and keep the phone level so the walls and doorways stay upright. Start wide to show the whole chamber, then pick one niche or doorway and fill the frame with its bone pattern. Tilt up for the vault fresco. Leave a little space around the subject so people walking through don't clip the edges.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bones to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so lit areas don't wash out. Indoors, hold still and let night mode work if your phone offers it; brace your elbows against your body. Panorama is not worth using in such a small space.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daytime is the easiest for the façade. Inside, the light is mostly the church's own, so the time of day matters less, but check the official site for when it is open.

text.access_note: This is a church and a place of worship with an ossuary, so dress and behave respectfully, and check the official site before you go for opening arrangements and any photography rules.
claims_not_in_sources: Photography may be restricted or discouraged inside the church and ossuary.
The ossuary interior is small and dimly lit, mostly by artificial light.
The church stands on a built-up street, so the façade is best photographed from the pavement opposite or a little way back.
The ossuary is a place where visitors are expected to be quiet and respectful.
Daylight is easier for photographing the façade.

name: Piazza Gae Aulenti and Porta Nuova
label: Gae Aulenti
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Piazza Gae Aulenti' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Piazza Gae Aulenti' (way/724414223): middle (335 m across).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q3906910 (coordinate location).

text.description:
Piazza Gae Aulenti is a raised, circular, pedestrian square about 100 metres across, in Milan's Isola neighbourhood and right in front of Porta Garibaldi station. César Pelli designed it to complement the skyscrapers next to it, and it opened on 8 December 2012. It is named after the Italian architect and designer Gae Aulenti. The tallest of those towers is the UniCredit Tower, at 231 metres the tallest skyscraper in Italy.

It photographs well for two reasons. The square is lifted well above the surrounding streets, so you get a wide, open view of the skyline. It also has three large fountain pools, which give you water in the foreground. From the east ramp up to the upper ring, look back over the pools. The UniCredit Tower sits on the right of the frame and the Bosco Verticale towers in the centre-left. Guides often call this the postcard view of the district.

The Bosco Verticale towers are private apartments, so you photograph them from outside only. If you want a cleaner shot of both towers, the Biblioteca degli Alberi park makes a good second stop, with young trees and a clean green foreground. Via Gaetano de Castillia shows the towers together at full height. On a phone, keep the horizon level, use the gridlines and leave a little sky above the tallest tower. The square can host stands and events, so the layout may change from day to day.
text.geographic_location: In the Isola neighbourhood of Milan, in front of the entrance to Porta Garibaldi station and just outside the eastern edge of the Milan Business Center. The Biblioteca degli Alberi park is next door.
text.directions_text: Take Metro line M2 or M5 to Garibaldi FS; the square is about 3 minutes on foot to the east. Trams 10 and 33 stop at Stazione Garibaldi M2 M5, also about 3 minutes on foot away. From Gioia (Metro line M2) it is about 7 minutes on foot, heading west. The phone icon on the map is on the eastern side of the square, where the ramp rises to the upper ring. The phone icon on the map is about 65 m east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the pools, the UniCredit Tower and the Bosco Verticale together. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched view. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the tree-covered balconies on the Bosco Verticale towers.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 65 m east of the subject, in Piazza Gae Aulenti (the phone icon on the map), and face west. On the east ramp up to the upper ring, and turn to shoot back over the fountain pools. From here the pools reflect the UniCredit Tower on the right of the frame, with Bosco Verticale in the centre-left.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put the water in the lower third so its reflections lead the eye up to the towers. Turn on the gridlines to keep the vertical lines straight, and avoid tilting the phone upwards. For a different view, Biblioteca degli Alberi frames both Bosco Verticale towers with trees in front.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the towers to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour. At blue hour, use night mode and brace your elbows against your body or rest the phone on a ledge to keep it steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Blue hour, according to one guide, when the towers are lit and the sky still has colour. For Bosco Verticale from Via Gaetano de Castillia, sunrise lights the towers from behind. Sunrise and sunset times change through the year, so check them before you go.

text.access_note: The square is a pedestrian public space; the Bosco Verticale towers are private apartments and can only be photographed from outside, and for any events or special set-ups check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Keeping the phone level and using gridlines helps keep the tall buildings' vertical lines straight.
Resting your elbows or the phone on a ledge helps keep night-mode shots steady.
Reflections in the pools are clearest when the water is calm.

name: Torre Velasca
label: Torre Velasca
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Piazza Velasca' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Piazza Velasca' (relation/19086632): middle (140 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/18238298: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Torre Velasca' (73 m across).

text.description:
Torre Velasca is the mushroom-shaped tower just south of Milan's Duomo, and it is one of the most distinctive outlines in the city. The architects BBPR finished it in 1958 and it was inaugurated in 1961. It rises 26 storeys, about 106 metres to the roof. The top floors sit wider than the base and are held out by exposed diagonal supports. The design echoes the overhanging towers of medieval Lombard fortresses, translated into reinforced concrete with stone cladding. Milanese people nicknamed it "the skyscraper with braces", and it was placed under historic protection in 2011.

It photographs well because the shape is so unusual. From the foot of the tower you look straight up at the overhanging crown, and the heavy geometry fills the frame. Step back across the piazza and the whole building fits in with the streets around it. The tower is mixed-use, with homes and offices, so treat it as something to photograph from outside.

For a phone, make two or three different shots: a close, dramatic look upwards, a wider shot with the square and passers-by for scale, and a tighter crop of the crown alone. If you want the tower in the wider cityscape, the Duomo's rooftops give a view across the old centre with the spires in the foreground. Check the official site before you go if you plan to go up there.
text.geographic_location: Torre Velasca stands in the centre of Milan, a short walk south of the Duomo, between Corso di Porta Romana and Via Larga. It is right beside Missori Metro station.
text.directions_text: Take Metro line M3 to Missori Metro station. One of its exits is right in front of the tower, and it is about 2 minutes on foot to the phone icon on the map. By tram, the Missori M3 stop (trams 12, 16, 19 and 24) is also about 2 minutes on foot away. From the Duomo, walk south for a short stroll to Piazza Velasca. The phone icon on the map is about 15 m west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) at the base of the tower to capture the whole overhanging crown above you. Switch to the default lens (1x) once you step back across the piazza. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to crop in on the crown and its diagonal supports.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 15 m west of the subject, in Piazza Velasca (the phone icon on the map), and face east. From here you look up at the overhanging upper floors and the bold concrete crown from ground level. Step back for a wider view with the piazza in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the tower's edges up with the vertical lines so it doesn't look as though it is toppling over. Keep the crown as the main subject and let people crossing the piazza give a sense of scale. If you want the tower among the city's rooftops, the Duomo rooftop is an alternative viewpoint, with the Duomo's spires in the foreground; there, zoom in with the telephoto lens.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky or the lighter part of the crown to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the concrete keeps its detail and the sky does not turn white. Hold the phone level, because tilting it upward makes the walls lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Golden hour or early morning give softer light and fewer people in the square.

text.access_note: Piazza Velasca is an open public square, but the tower itself is a working building, so do not count on getting inside; check the official site before you go, and likewise for the Duomo rooftop.
claims_not_in_sources: Piazza Velasca is an open public square that can be visited at any time.
Building works or renovation around the base of the tower may partly block the view.
The Duomo rooftop requires a ticket, so visitors should check the official site.
Tilting a phone upwards makes tall buildings appear to lean inwards, which gridlines can help correct.
Golden hour and early morning give softer light and fewer people.

name: Piazza Mercanti
label: Piazza Mercanti
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Loggia degli Osii' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Loggia degli Osii' (way/435768737): middle (28 m across); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/10057932: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Piazza dei Mercanti' (103 m across).

text.description:
Piazza Mercanti is a small, calm square in the middle of Milan, tucked between the Duomo and Piazza Cordusio. In the Middle Ages it was the heart of the city, and the buildings around it still show that. The brick arcades of the Palazzo della Ragione, built in 1233 as the city's administrative seat, fill the north-eastern side. On the south-eastern side stands the Loggia degli Osii, built in 1316 for Matteo I Visconti, with the balcony from which the authorities once spoke to the crowd. In the centre is a 16th-century well topped with two 18th-century columns.

For a phone photo, the appeal is in the details. Arches repeat, the brick and stone have texture, and the Palazzo della Ragione carries two well-known reliefs, one of a boar and one of Oldrado da Tresseno, who ordered the palace built. Standing in front of the Loggia degli Osii gives you a quieter, closer view of its arcades and carved front, rather than the wide square. If you want the wider picture too, step into the middle for the arcades with the old well in the foreground, or look through the arches of the Palazzo della Ragione.

Take your time and keep to the edges of the paths so others can pass. Restoration work has sometimes put scaffolding on the buildings, so what you see may vary on the day.
text.geographic_location: In the historic centre of Milan, on the short stretch between Piazza del Duomo and Piazza Cordusio. It is a very short walk from the Duomo.
text.directions_text: From Duomo Metro station (Metro line M1 and Metro line M3) the square lies to the west, about 2 minutes on foot. From Cordusio Metro station (Metro line M1) it lies to the south-east, also about 2 minutes on foot. The nearest tram stop is Via Orefici - Piazza Cordusio (tram 12, tram 14, tram 16, tram 19 and tram 2), about 1 minute on foot to the south-west of the square. The phone icon on the map is about 20 m south of the numbered pin. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the loggia's arcades and front. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the arcade in frame, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the carved details and the reliefs across the square.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 20 m south of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. From here you see the loggia's arcades and the relief decoration on its front, with the middle of the square to the north-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the arch columns with the vertical lines so the arcade looks straight. Fill the frame with the arches and carvings for a detail-focused shot. For a wider view, walk into the square and include the old well in the foreground, with the brick arcades of the Palazzo della Ragione behind it. Looking through the arches of the Palazzo della Ragione is another good frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the carvings keep their detail. Hold the phone level and avoid tilting it upwards, or the buildings will lean inwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the day is likely to be quieter. Soft, even daylight suits the brick and carved stone, and it is worth checking on site whether scaffolding is up.

text.access_note: The square is an open public space where photography is generally free, but for any building interiors or special openings, check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Early in the day the square is likely to be quieter than later on.
Soft, even daylight tends to suit brick and carved stone.
From in front of the Loggia degli Osii, a telephoto lens can pick out details of the buildings across the square.
Tilting the phone upwards makes buildings appear to lean inwards.

name: Pirelli Tower
label: Pirelli Tower
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Piazza Duca d'Aosta' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Piazza Duca d'Aosta' (relation/1322178): middle (267 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/89444196: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Pirelli Tower' (74 m across).

text.description:
The Pirelli Tower, known locally as the Pirellone ('Big Pirelli'), is a slim 32-storey skyscraper next to Milan's main railway station. It rises 127 m and was finished in 1958, designed by Gio Ponti with Pier Luigi Nervi and Arturo Danusso. It was built on the site of the Pirelli company's first factory, and it came to stand for Milan's recovery after the war. The sides taper in, and the walls are mostly glass hung on a structural frame. That made it one of the first skyscrapers to move away from the plain box shape. The Lombardy regional government has owned it since 1978.

It photographs well because the shape is so clean. The long, narrow facade makes a strong vertical line against the sky, and the pointed ends give you a distinctive outline. The best-known view is from Piazza Duca d'Aosta, the square in front of the main facade, directly opposite Milano Centrale. From there the tower fills the frame above the square. You face west to shoot it, so the station is behind you. At about 160 m away the tower is tall in the frame, and the ultra-wide lens helps fit it all in. Keep the phone upright and level so the sides stay straight. If you have time, walk round to Via Galvani for a less familiar view of the back of the tower, but check on the spot that it works.
text.geographic_location: The Pirelli Tower stands next to Milano Centrale station, just west of it. Piazza Duca d'Aosta is the square between the station and the tower. Gioia Metro station is about 500 m away.
text.directions_text: Take Metro line M2 or M3 to Centrale FS Metro station; the phone icon on the map is about 2 minutes on foot from there, and the tower is to the west. Trams 9 and 10 stop very close by at Via Filzi - Via Galvani and Via Filzi Via Pirelli. From the phone icon on the map the tower is a short stroll west, about 3 minutes on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 140 m east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole tower in from where you stand, about 160 m away. Use the default lens (1x) if you can stand further back and want less stretching at the edges.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 140 m east of the subject, in Piazza Duca d'Aosta (the phone icon on the map), and face west. Face west and you see the broad main facade rising above the square, with the station behind you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn the phone upright (portrait) and use the gridlines to line the sides of the tower up with the vertical grid lines. Keep the phone level rather than tilting it up, as tilting makes the building lean. Leave a little sky above the top, and include some of the square at the bottom to show scale. For a different angle, try the back of the tower from Via Galvani, but check on the spot that the view works.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the glass facade to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky keeps its colour and the building does not wash out. Try a 2x shot to pick out the top of the tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters the glass. Early evening, as the sky darkens and the lights come on, can also work well; use night mode and hold the phone steady against something solid.

text.access_note: The square in front of the tower is a public open space; the tower itself is a government office building, and its top-floor viewing level opens only on certain days, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Piazza Duca d'Aosta is an open public square you can stand in without a ticket.
The ultra-wide lens (0.5x) helps fit a tall building into the frame when you are standing close.
Tilting the phone upward makes vertical lines lean inwards.
Morning or late-afternoon light, or the early evening blue hour, tends to flatter a glass facade.
Night mode works best when the phone is held steady against something solid.

name: Duomo rooftop terraces
label: Duomo rooftop
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/18017026: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Milan Cathedral' (180 m across).
notes: Photographed on the roof itself (ticketed: check the official site).

text.description:
Milan Cathedral is the city's great Gothic landmark, and its roof gives you something the square below cannot: the building close up. Spires, pinnacles and carved figures stand in rows around you, all in pale marble, with the city spread out beyond. That mix of fine detail in the foreground and rooftops in the distance is what makes the spot work so well for phone photos.

The cathedral took nearly six centuries to finish. Building began in 1386, and the final details were completed in 1965. It is the largest church in Italy and one of the largest in the world. Among its details is the Guglietto dell'Amadeo, a small Renaissance spire built between 1507 and 1510 that still sits comfortably with the Gothic style. The octagonal cupola was completed between 1500 and 1510.

On the roof, look for repeating lines: rows of spires, flying buttresses and statues that lead the eye into the frame. Put one carved figure or spire close to the lens and let the skyline sit behind it. Keep your phone away from the edges of the terraces, hold it with both hands, and take a few frames of each view, because people often drift into the shot. Wipe the lens first; marble dust and fingerprints soften the image more than you would expect.
text.geographic_location: In the very centre of Milan, on the roof of Milan Cathedral. Cordusio Metro station lies a short walk away.
text.directions_text: Take Metro line M1 or M3 to Duomo Metro station, which is about 3 minutes on foot from the cathedral, with the cathedral to the east. Alternatively, tram 24 or tram 27 stops at Piazza Fontana, about 3 minutes on foot away, with the cathedral to the north-west. From Cordusio Metro station on line M1 it is about 7 minutes on foot. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for sweeping views of the spires, but keep the edges clear of people or railings, as it stretches anything close to the lens. The default lens (1x) suits most roof views. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out statues, carved details and distant landmarks.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Take your photos from the roof terraces, with the spires and marble figures close by.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place a spire or statue on one of the lines, with the city skyline behind it. Shoot the same view at 1x and at 2x or more, because the tighter version often shows the carving best. For a wide sweep along the roofline, try panorama mode and move slowly.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the marble to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the pale stone looks washed out against the sky. Portrait mode can work for a friend standing near a spire, but check that the edges around the stonework look clean.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early or late in the day usually gives softer light on the marble and fewer harsh shadows. Midday sun can make the stone glare, so use the exposure slider if you are there then.

text.access_note: The roof terraces are part of the cathedral, so access may be ticketed or restricted; check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The cathedral's roof terraces can be visited, and access may need a ticket or timed entry.
From the roof you can see spires, buttresses and statues close up, with the city skyline beyond.
Early or late in the day usually gives softer light on pale marble than midday sun.
Other visitors on the roof often wander into photos.
